_comment: Numbers in prose, pinned to a resolver that re-derives them from the repository.
Read by scripts/check-counts.mjs. Each entry names a document, a regex with exactly
one capture group around the number, a resolver, and why the number is worth guarding.
Two rules, matching scripts/catalog-known-defects.json and divergence-allowlist.json:
- an entry whose pattern matches nothing FAILS AS STALE, so a pin cannot outlive
- every occurrence of a pattern must agree, because a number repeated three times
is three chances to be wrong and '673-paper corpus' was exactly that.
Pin a number when being wrong about it would change a decision. Do not pin every
digit in the documentation — a pin file nobody can read is one nobody maintains.

claims.reason: The corpus is the stated warrant for the four measured results this ADR opens with. It said '673-paper corpus' three times; the tree holds 661 files and 599 unique documents. A warrant nobody can reproduce is not one.
Same claim, restated twice more in the corpus document itself — the place a reader would go to check it.
The file count and the document count differ by 62 byte-identical duplicates. Stating only one of them is how 599 got rounded up to 673.
This comment justifies ignoring the corpus. It said 906 MB against a measured 2,081 — the same drift class as the documentation, in a file that changes behaviour.
Said 180; the registry holds 195. check:plan already reports 195, so the repository knew and the ADR did not.
Action item 7 sizes future work off this number.
The 'catalog is a hypothesis space' argument counts the hypotheses.
The status table is the first thing a reader trusts.

claims.pattern: records behind a pure registry — ([\d,]+) frozen
claims.reason: 172 frozen records, from the frozen catalog rather than from memory.
Said 8 added; 23 were. The gap between 172 and 195 is exactly what this number is supposed to explain.
The plan's PROSE contradicted the plan's own machine-checked JSON block, which check:plan reads instead. Two claims, one document, one checker covering only one of them.
Same sentence, second wrong number.
Same sentence, third number — and the one check:plan's JSON block gets right, which is what makes the prose contradiction worth catching.

ADR-0008 names this partition 'the routing rule' deciding which cases may reach a judge. A stale partition is a stale rule, not a cosmetic count — this is the single highest-consequence number in the documentation.
The judge-routed share grew 25% (8 to 10) while the documented figure stood still. Judge calls are the expensive, biased path the rule exists to bound.
Completes the partition. Three numbers that must sum to the catalog size, checked separately so the sum cannot hide a compensating error.
True today, and pinned deliberately: a pin file containing only broken claims proves the checker fires, never that it stays quiet when it should.
Second currently-true pin, in a different document, for the same must-not-fire reason.
CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session, so a wrong number here misleads before any file is read. It said 26; there are 31.
Third currently-true pin. Also the number CLAUDE.md is most likely to be trusted on without checking.

The Codex-facing sibling of CLAUDE.md, and it drifted for exactly the reason CLAUDE.md is pinned: loaded into every session, believed before any file is read. It said 37 while there were 43, and was invisible to this checker because it was untracked.
Same sentence, same file, same hazard as the CLAUDE.md pin above it.
The README's tree table. A reader counting schemas is deciding whether the contract set is small enough to read, so a stale figure changes a judgement.
Restated in the README's headline figures. Two statements of one number are two chances to be wrong, which is what this file exists for.
The gate count is the most-cited figure in the project and was wrong in four documents before check:counts existed.
The pipeline grew from nine stages to eleven mid-project; a loose copy in a README is exactly how the old number survives.
Stated as 180 in four documents while the registry held 195. The README must not become the fifth.
599 unique documents, not the 661 files or the 673 that three documents claimed.
Appears three times in the README with three different phrasings. Every occurrence must agree, which is the rule that catches a partial edit.
The file count and the document count differ by 62 byte-identical duplicates; stating only one of them is how 599 got rounded up.

The headline gate count, in the file a new session reads first. Three source comments claiming '2 of 16 ported' survived every guard while all 16 were, so this number has already been wrong in this repository.
The same count restated in the directory map. A number repeated twice is two chances to be wrong, and the check requires both occurrences to agree.
Said 32 the day two ADRs landed. Cheap to re-derive, and wrong here means a reader thinks they have seen the whole doc set.
Stated twice in this file and wrong in both the moment ADR-0010 and 0011 landed. An ADR index that undercounts hides the decisions a reader most needs.
Contracts are the sole cross-boundary interface, so their count is the size of the interface. Restated in the quick facts and the directory map; both must agree.
The stage count moved from nine to eleven once already, and a doc set that never mentioned the two new stages is the reason check:stages exists.
'The allowlist ships with zero entries and that is correct' was true, quoted, and load-bearing right up until it was not.
The opening line of the contracts reference. If it disagrees with the index, one of the two is lying to whoever reads only one.
The heading over the gate table. A heading that says sixteen above a table of fifteen rows is the failure this catches.
The open register said Five while the spec held twelve. The register is where a reader goes to learn what is still wrong, so a stale count there understates the residue by more than half.

Risk register R2 said "zero entries, which is correct" for a week after the count reached four. R2 is the row asserting the oracle has not been silenced, so a wrong number there undercuts the mitigation it claims.

The count of local model fingerprints observed and pinned. Four places now state it in prose, and it is exactly the number that grows the next time somebody runs a model and does not grow in the docs — the shape every wrong count in this file had. Derived from scripts/model-fingerprints.json, the file the fingerprint watch itself reads, so the documentation and the guard cannot disagree about how many models have answered.
